prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, Square, And

outputs.L1:
There once was a Square—a most proper little Square—  
Who cherished a neat little Triangle;  
But she was a flirt, and about her skirt  
She let him hopelessly dangle.  

Oh, he longed to wed, and he felt no dread  
Of domestic woes or wrangles;  
For he dreamed that his fate was to procreate  
Dear little Squares and Triangles.  

Now, it happened one day, along that geometric way,  
There swaggered a bold, imposing Cube;  
With a haughty stare, he made that Square  
Appear the perfect boob.  

To his solid spell the Triangle fell,  
And she thrilled with love’s sweet sickness;  
For she delighted in his breadth and height—  
But how she adored his thickness!  

So the poor little Square simply died of despair,  
For his love he could not strangle;  
While the bold Cube led to the bridal bed  
That cute and acute Triangle.  

The Square’s sad lot she has long since forgot,  
Along with his passionate pretensions;  
For now she dotes on her children—oh, such charming Pyramids—  
In a world of three dimensions.
outputs.L2:
Once there was a very small Square, neat and precise, who fell deeply in love with a shapely Triangle. But the Triangle was playful and teasing, and she kept him hopelessly trailing after her without returning his devotion.

The Square longed to marry her and was not afraid of the quarrels or troubles that might come with married life. He imagined their future together, picturing themselves as parents of charming little Squares and Triangles.

Then, one day, along that mathematical path, a large, confident Cube appeared. He strutted in boldly, looking so proud and impressive that the poor Square seemed foolish by comparison. The Triangle quickly came under the Cube’s powerful attraction and was overcome with romantic excitement. She admired his width and his height—but most of all, she was enchanted by his depth.

The unhappy Square was crushed by grief, unable to extinguish his love for her. Meanwhile, the daring Cube carried the pretty, sharp-angled Triangle off to marriage.

In time, the Triangle completely forgot the Square’s sorrow and his ardent hopes. Now she adores her children—adorable little Pyramids—living happily in a three-dimensional world.
outputs.L3:
A Square once fell deeply in love with a flirtatious Triangle. To him, she was graceful, lively, and charming, and he admired the way she seemed to catch everyone’s attention wherever she went. Although she often enjoyed the admiration of others, the Square believed his devotion would win her heart. He hoped that one day she would agree to marry him and share a life by his side.

In his imagination, the Square pictured a happy future together. He dreamed of a home filled with children who resembled them both—some with the steady, balanced form of Squares like himself, and others with the sharp, elegant shape of Triangles like their mother. These thoughts filled him with joy, and he cherished the idea that his love for the Triangle might grow into a family.

But one day, a bold and confident Cube appeared. Unlike the Square, the Cube possessed a striking three-dimensional presence. He had depth, volume, and an impressive solidity that immediately captured the Triangle’s interest. The Cube’s unusual qualities made him seem exciting and powerful, and the Triangle found herself drawn to him.

Before long, the Triangle chose the Cube instead of the devoted Square. The Square was left heartbroken, watching as the future he had imagined disappeared. His hopes of marriage, family, and lasting happiness with the Triangle were replaced by sadness and disappointment.

In time, the Triangle built a new life with the Cube. Together, they had children shaped like Pyramids, a blend of her triangular nature and his three-dimensional form. As the years passed, the Triangle became absorbed in her new family and gradually forgot the Square’s devotion. The Square’s love, once so sincere and hopeful, remained only a painful memory for him.
outputs.L4:
In the quiet plane of Paperland, where every figure lay flat beneath the mild white sky, there lived a careful Square. He was neat, dependable, and perfectly equal on every side. His corners were honest right angles, his borders clean and straight, and he believed that love, like geometry, ought to be balanced.

For many days he admired a graceful Triangle who lived just beyond the ruled blue margin. She was bright and sharp and lively, with three elegant sides and a point that seemed always to be looking upward. To the Square, she was the finest shape in all the plane.

At last, gathering his four corners of courage, he slid across the page to speak to her.

“Dear Triangle,” said the Square, bowing as well as a flat figure could, “I know I have more sides than you, but I hope you will not think me too complicated. My angles are steady, my sides are true, and my heart is as square as my shape. Will you let me court you?”

The Triangle tilted slightly, amused by his formality.

“You are very kind,” she said. “And very regular.”

The Square blushed along all four edges.

“I could offer you a life of symmetry,” he continued. “Together we could make patterns, tessellations, perhaps even a fine little house drawn neatly in perspective.”

“That sounds pleasant,” said the Triangle.

Encouraged, the Square began visiting every afternoon. He brought her rhombuses of folded paper, sang songs about parallel lines, and recited verses in which every stanza had four lines, because he thought that was most proper. He praised her points, admired her angles, and told her that though she had only three sides, she was complete in his eyes.

For a while, the Triangle smiled at his devotion. Yet sometimes, when the Square spoke of their future, her gaze drifted toward the edge of the paper, where the flat world seemed to end.

Then one day a shadow fell across the plane.

It was not the shadow of a line, nor of a circle, nor of any ordinary flat figure. It was deep, broad, and solid. The Square looked up—or tried to, though “up” was not a direction he used very often—and saw an astonishing stranger descending into Paperland.

He had six faces, eight vertices, and twelve bold edges. He was a Cube.

The Cube did not merely slide; he stood. He did not merely occupy space; he commanded it. Every face of him was a square, but multiplied into magnificence. He had depth, height, and breadth. He cast shade. He caught light. He could be turned and viewed from many sides, and each side promised another.

The Square stared in alarm.

The Triangle stared in wonder.

“Good afternoon,” said the Cube, his voice resonant with volume.

The Square straightened himself. “Sir, you appear to be trespassing on a two-dimensional courtship.”

“A thousand apologies,” replied the Cube. “I did not mean to intrude. I was merely passing through from the Third Dimension.”

“The Third Dimension?” whispered the Triangle.

The Cube smiled. “A place where shapes do not only lie flat. They rise. They deepen. They become bodies.”

The Square frowned. “There is nothing wrong with being flat. Flatness has many advantages. It is simple, elegant, and very easy to measure.”

“Certainly,” said the Cube politely. “I began with squares myself.”

This remark troubled the Square greatly. He could not deny the resemblance. The Cube was, in a sense, made of squares—but squares with grandeur, squares with ambition, squares that had somehow stepped out of the page and become architecture.

The Triangle turned to the Cube. “And what would become of a triangle in your dimension?”

“Ah,” said the Cube. “A triangle might become part of a pyramid. It might lift itself into space, meet other triangles, and rise to a point beneath the sun.”

The Triangle’s eyes shone.

The Square felt his corners stiffen.

“My dear Triangle,” he said quickly, “please consider. A pyramid sounds impressive, but it is also rather pointed. Our life together would be orderly. Predictable. Flat, yes, but safe.”

“Safe is not always enough,” said the Triangle gently.

The Square tried again. “But I love you in two dimensions.”

“And I thank you for it,” said the Triangle. “You have been kind and constant. But I think I was always meant to rise.”

The Cube extended one sturdy edge like an arm.

“Would you like to see beyond the plane?” he asked.

The Triangle looked once at the Square, with affection but not with love, and then stepped toward the Cube.

There was a fold in the world, a sudden shift of perspective, and the Triangle was no longer merely a flat figure on the page. She became a face among faces, part of something higher, something with height and shadow and space. The Square watched as she entered the Third Dimension and became the proud companion of the Cube.

In time, they had children: little Pyramids, each with triangular faces and sharp bright peaks. They tumbled through space, casting charming shadows and making the most delightful three-dimensional mischief. The Triangle adored them. The Cube, naturally, was very proud.

As for the Square, he remained in Paperland. For a while he was quite heartbroken and lay at a melancholy angle across the page. But eventually he took comfort in his own virtues. He became a window, then a tile, then part of a handsome checkerboard. He even discovered that there were other shapes who admired stability, symmetry, and a good right angle.

Still, whenever a shadow passed over the paper, he would think of the Triangle and the Cube, and he would sigh along one side.

For he had learned a difficult lesson: in matters of love, four equal sides may be admirable, but sometimes the heart longs for depth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a humorous old-fashioned narrative poem about a Square in love with a Triangle who leaves him for a Cube, ending with their children being Pyramids.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Square, the Triangle, and the Cube**

In days when ink was stout and black,  
And candles wore a sputtering knack,  
There lived, upon a paper plain,  
A Square of most punctilious grain.

Four honest sides, four angles true,  
His waistcoat pressed, his corners blue;  
He paid his rent, he swept his floor,  
And never leaned against a door.

Yet though his life was neat and spare,  
A sorrow lodged within the Square:  
For down the lane, with graceful angle,  
There dwelt a most bewitching Triangle.

Her hat was sharp, her laugh acute,  
Her manners airy, arch, and cute;  
She danced a jig on point and toe  
That made the Square’s diagonals glow.

“Dear Miss,” said he, “my heart is thine;  
Pray be my own, and share my line.  
I’ve four good walls, a tidy view,  
And room enough for me and you.”

The Triangle smiled a slanting smile,  
And kept him hopeful for a while;  
She took his flowers, his cakes, his chalk,  
And let him escort her on a walk.

But ah! one day, with pomp and tube,  
There rolled to town a wealthy Cube—  
A solid chap of depth and dash,  
With six broad faces and a moustache.

He had, besides his front and back,  
A cellar, loft, and luggage rack;  
He boasted volume, girth, and grace,  
And occupied a deal of space.

The Triangle gazed, and softly cried,  
“What breadth! What height! What underside!”  
The Square turned pale as paper paste;  
His angles trembled at the waist.

“Farewell,” she said, “you’re good and fair,  
But far too flat, my dearest Square.  
A lady must, when all is done,  
Prefer dimension more than one.”

She wed the Cube at half-past eight;  
The compass served them on a plate.  
The Protractor gave away the bride;  
The Rhombus sniffed and nearly cried.

The Square looked on with dignified pain,  
Then folded up and walked in rain.  
He muttered, “Love is but a sum  
Where I am naught, and he is plumb.”

The years rolled by; the Square grew wise,  
And wore small spectacles on his eyes.  
He taught young shapes their A-B-Cs  
And warned them all of threes and she’s.

Then news arrived by graph and grid  
Of what the Cube and Triangle did:  
They’d settled down, as proud as squires,  
And filled their house with little spires.

Their children, bright in sunlit beams,  
Were Pyramids with lofty dreams—  
With triangular faces, square-ish floor,  
And points that scratched the nursery door.

The Square, upon receiving this,  
Observed, “A most peculiar bliss!  
She left me flat, the faithless madam,  
Yet kept a Square about the bottom.”

And so he laughed, though love had stung,  
And kept his corners ever young;  
For in geometry, as in men,  
What goes around comes round again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a witty rhyming poem using geometric shapes as characters in a love triangle, with puns about dimensions and “cute/acute” angles.
counterfactuals.output:
In Polygon Park by the axis of y,  
A Circle met Triangle and let out a sigh.  
“You’re looking quite sharp,” she said with a smile,  
“Those angles of yours are acute by a mile.”

But Square, standing there with his four equal sides,  
Felt corners of jealousy poking his pride.  
“I’m stable! I’m solid! I’m perfectly true—  
And honestly, Circle, I’m a-round just for you.”

Triangle winked, “Don’t be obtuse, my dear,  
Our chemistry’s plane, but the feeling is clear.  
She likes how I’m edgy, dimensional, neat—  
My angles aren’t just acute, they’re cute.”

Circle blushed red as a compass-drawn rose,  
“I’m drawn to you both, as geometry goes.  
Square gives me structure, so steady and fine,  
But Triangle’s points make my heart intersect lines.”

Square sighed, “This love’s gone from two-D to tense—  
I’m losing my area, sense, and defense.”  
Triangle said, “Face it, our fate’s not so square;  
Love’s a theorem with proof in the air.”

Then Circle declared, with a spin and a twirl,  
“No need to be warped in this Euclidean whirl.  
Let’s not be divided by edges or hue—  
There’s infinite space in my heart for you two.”

So Square took a corner, Triangle took three,  
And Circle embraced them in symmetry.  
Their romance, though odd, had a perfect connection:  
A love triangle with well-rounded affection.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a comic ballad in the style of early 20th-century light verse about a flat Square, a flirtatious Triangle, and a bold three-dimensional Cube.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ballad of Square, Triangle, and Cube**

In Euclid’s neat and polished town,  
Where angles all were true,  
There dwelt a most respectable Square,  
Of proper moral hue.  

He wore four sides of equal cut,  
Four corners starched and prim;  
His life was ruled by parallel lines,  
And parallel were him.  

Each morning at precisely eight  
He swept his little plane,  
And murmured, “Order, breadth, and length—  
The rest is quite inane.”  

But down the street, with tilted point  
And most coquettish angle,  
There tripped a lively Triangle  
Who set the town a-jangle.  

Her hem was cut on bias-lines,  
Her vertex nodded sly;  
She’d wink one angle at the Square  
And turn the others by.  

“Oh, Mister Square,” she softly sang,  
“How dreadfully you plod!  
A figure with so many rules  
Is positively odd.”  

“I am not odd,” the Square replied,  
“My sides are even, miss.  
And I object, on moral grounds,  
To vertices that kiss.”  

She laughed a little tinkling laugh,  
And spun upon one side.  
“Then walk with me beyond the line—  
The plane is much too wide!”  

The Square grew pink along his edge,  
His corners quivered sore;  
He’d never left his paper street,  
Nor wished to, much, before.  

Just then there came a thumping sound,  
A shadow crossed the view;  
And into Flatland’s fragile calm  
There strode a booming Cube.  

He had six faces, broad and bold,  
Twelve edges, every one;  
Eight lordly corners polished bright  
And glinting in the sun.  

“Good day!” he cried. “What charming flats!  
How quaintly thin you are!  
I’ve travelled down from Higher Space—  
It’s really not so far.”  

The Triangle clasped all three hands—  
At least, she tried her best—  
And simpered, “Sir, your depth of soul  
Surpasses all the rest.”  

The Square drew up his equal sides  
And gave a frosty cough.  
“Your thickness, sir, is not the sort  
We commonly approve of.”  

“Nonsense!” the Cube cried jovially,  
“I’ll show you something grand.  
A little height, a touch of depth—  
Why, you can understand!”  

He lifted Square clean off the plane;  
Poor Square began to squeal:  
“My area! My bearings! Stop!  
I’m feeling far too real!”  

They soared above the dotted streets,  
Past circles, lines, and arcs;  
The Triangle blew kisses down  
And made improving remarks.  

“Observe,” the Cube said, “from up here,  
Your world is like a sheet.”  
The Square looked down and faintly gasped,  
Then landed on his feet.  

For there, revealed in shocking truth,  
Was every private fence,  
Each polygon’s back garden plot,  
Each circle’s false pretence.  

The Square beheld his own roofline—  
He’d never known he had one—  
And cried, “Existence, I admit,  
Is rather more than flat one!”  

The Triangle clapped merrily.  
“I told you life was wide!”  
“And tall,” the Cube remarked with pride,  
“And pleasantly inside.”  

But gossip travels very fast  
In geometric nations;  
By tea-time all the pentagons  
Were faint with speculations.  

“The Square has been uplifted!” cried  
A rhombus in a swoon.  
“A Triangle encouraged it—  
They’ll all be solids soon!”  

The Square returned at half-past four  
A wiser, wobblier man;  
He locked his gate with trembling line  
And drew a careful plan.  

The Triangle came pirouetting,  
Bright as a theorem’s spark.  
“Do call again,” she said to Cube.  
“I’m free from dawn till dark.”  

The Cube bowed low—too low, in fact,  
And dented half the town;  
Then thundered off through Higher Space,  
Upside, inside, and down.  

The Square watched long, then sighed and spoke,  
His voice a little strange:  
“I still prefer four equal sides—  
But depth is not derange.”  

So if you meet a rigid Square  
Who scorns all things askew,  
Just whisper “Triangle,” then “Cube,”  
And watch him blush in blue.  

For angles prim and edges bold  
May yet be led to roam,  
And even the flattest heart may find  
A dimension out from home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a playful poem where a Square wants to marry a Triangle, but she falls for a Cube because of his “thickness,” and they have Pyramid children.
counterfactuals.output:
There once was a Square, so proper and neat,  
With four little corners and four equal feet.  
He loved a bright Triangle, sharp, witty, and slim,  
And dreamed she’d say “yes” and go dancing with him.

He brought her some flowers in polygon style,  
Arranged at right angles to win her sweet smile.  
He said, “We’d be perfect—our edges align!”  
She said, “You’re quite lovely… but not quite my kind.”

For into the room rolled a Cube with a grin,  
All depth and dimension and charm packed within.  
The Triangle swooned, blushed pink at the bricks—  
“Oh my,” she exclaimed, “he’s delightfully thick!”

The Square sighed, “But darling, I’m balanced! I’m flat!”  
She said, “Yes, dear Square, and there’s honor in that.  
But Cube has… perspective. He’s solid. He’s true.  
He’s got that extra something I never saw in you.”

So Cube and Triangle were wed in the sun,  
With circles as guests and rectangles for fun.  
And soon came their children, all pointy and bright:  
Little Pyramid babies, a magical sight.

They toddled on bases, they giggled in stacks,  
With triangular faces and geometric knack.  
The Square came to visit and smiled through his tears,  
Then became Uncle Square for the next many years.

And though he still longed for that triangular spark,  
He found a sweet Rhombus one day in the park.  
So all shapes found joy, in their own special way—  
In love, as in math, there’s more than one plane.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical geometry-themed romance poem full of shape puns, rhymes, and a tragic Square losing his beloved Triangle to a Cube.
counterfactuals.output:
In Polygon Town, where the angles all gleam,  
Lived Square, with a perfectly measured-up dream.  
His edges were honest, his corners were true,  
And his heart made a right angle whenever love grew.

He courted Miss Triangle, sharp, graceful, acute,  
With a vertexy smile and a hypotenuse suit.  
He said, “You’re so a-cute, dear, it’s plane to see—  
You’re the missing dimension in my geometry.”

She blushed, “Oh, Square, you’re so stable and fair,  
So equal, so steady, so wonderfully... square.”  
They danced in the moonlight, congruent in pace,  
Two figures in love in a two-dimensional space.

But alas! From the shadows, with volume and flair,  
Came Cube in a carriage of isometric air.  
He had depth. He had height. He had six flashy sides.  
He said, “Why live flat when you could take spacious rides?”

Triangle gasped, “He’s solid! He’s rich! He’s profound!”  
Square cried, “But my love is the best shape around!”  
Cube smirked, “Little quadrilateral, don’t be obtuse—  
She’s tired of flat dates and your area excuse.”

Square shouted, “You blockhead! You boxed-up buffoon!  
You’ll prism her away before next waxing moon!”  
But Triangle sighed, “Square, don’t take it so hard—  
You’re four-cornered sweetness, but life needs a yard.”

“A yard?” Square went pale. “That’s a line of attack!  
You’re leaving me now for a six-sided hack?”  
She whispered, “Dear Square, please don’t be so mean;  
With Cube, I can finally live in 3-D.”

Then off rolled the Cube with his cubic allure,  
While Triangle waved, looking less than demure.  
Square stood there flattened, his perimeter cracked,  
A plane little lover by dimensions outflanked.

He measured his sorrow in units of pain,  
Drew circles of grief in the cold Cartesian rain.  
“My love was all right,” he cried, “right angles, all four—  
But she wanted much more than a square could afford.”

Now every night, under graph-paper skies,  
Square counts broken segments and quietly cries.  
For Triangle’s gone, and the lesson is cruel:  
In romance, dear shapes, volume often rules.

So pity poor Square, with his love misconstrued—  
Outclassed, outspaced, and three-dimensionally skewed.  
He was perfectly even, but fate had declared:  
Some hearts will be cubed, and some merely squared.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
